title: Product Sense Score

bands.name: Emerging
bands.tagline: Partial ORBIT, a lot of thrash

setup.prompt: Which is closest to your role?

options.text: Senior PM or above, in role
PM below senior
Engineer or designer leading product work
Founder
Something else

setup.prompt: What's the initiative you own going into planning?
setup.placeholder: self-serve onboarding for small business accounts
setup.help: Describe it the way you would to a peer at another company. No internal codename, no customer names, no numbers. I use this to write the questions around your actual work and to make the results about it. It's stored with your score and nothing else. Two questions ask you for a sentence; those are scored against my rubric by an AI model and are not used to train anything. Email me any time and I'll delete all of it.

instruction: These ask what actually happened. If a situation hasn't come up on [initiative] yet, pick what you'd most likely do.

questions.prompt: Think about the last time leadership asked where [initiative] was going next year. What did you actually bring?

options.text: A ranked list of the most requested improvements, with effort estimates.
A focus area, with the reasoning for why it mattered most.
A direction that named what we would not be doing next year, and why.
Options with the trade-offs laid out so leadership could choose.

questions.prompt: The last time a stakeholder pushed a feature onto [initiative] with "or we lose the deal," what did you do first?

options.text: Pulled the numbers to see how many deals were actually at risk.
Estimated it with engineering so I could give them a date.
Wrote down, in their words, what they believed the problem was, and checked it with the people closest to the deals.
Explained why it wasn't on the roadmap this quarter.

questions.prompt: The last time a debate about [initiative] went in circles (this feature versus that one), what did you do?

options.text: Kept it on the agenda and drove to a decision on the features.
Proposed we step back and agree which customer we're building for before ranking anything.
Said out loud what I thought the room was actually arguing about, named who would lose under the new frame, and offered them something.
Let it run; the data would settle it in a couple of weeks.

questions.prompt: When you last presented a trade-off on [initiative] and someone said "obviously option A," what did you take from it?

options.text: We had consensus; I documented it and moved on.
Option B wasn't real yet. I hadn't shown what a sane person gains by choosing it, so the decision would get reopened later by whoever did.
I should add a third option that split the difference.
They didn't understand the risk in A; I looped in my tech lead.

questions.prompt: Six weeks before your last launch on [initiative], who was actually aligned?

options.text: Engineering, design, and my manager; the rest we'd loop in at launch readiness.
Engineering, design, my manager, and marketing.
All of those plus finance or legal, because I had already asked each of them what would stop the launch.
Everyone who mattered; my manager handled their peers.

questions.prompt: When you last explained [initiative] to a room with a finance person, an engineer, and a salesperson in it, how did you handle it?

options.text: One version of the story for everyone; consistency matters.
Separate 1:1s beforehand, so the meeting was a formality.
One framing that named what each of them is measured on, and said what we were not doing so sales heard it from me first.
Kept it high level so nobody got into the weeds.

questions.prompt: The last time someone repeated your strategy for [initiative] back to you (a tech lead, a peer, your manager), how close was it?

options.text: Word for word, including what we were not doing.
The gist held; the details drifted.
They repeated the features, not the direction.
Nobody has had to; I'm in every meeting where it comes up.

questions.prompt: When you last had two minutes with an exec about [initiative], what did you open with?

options.text: The decision we're making, what it costs us, and the number it moves.
The customer problem, and how we found it.
The context on how we got here.
What the team has built so far.

written.prompt: In one sentence, write the direction you've set for [initiative].
written.placeholder: We are making checkout the fastest in the category for repeat buyers, which means we are not touching onboarding next year.

rubric.text: Names a choice that rules something out, and ties it to an outcome the company already measures.
A clear focus with a company outcome, but nothing ruled out.
A focus area or theme with no outcome ("make onboarding better").
A feature list, a mission statement, "improve [initiative]," or blank.

examples.text: Cut time-to-first-value for self-serve accounts from days to one session, so the 30-day activation number moves, which means no new admin features this year.
Make self-serve onboarding fast enough that 30-day activation goes up.
Improve the onboarding experience for new accounts.
Onboarding checklist, progress bar, welcome email series, and in-app tips.

written.prompt: In one sentence, what are you explicitly not doing on [initiative] this year?
written.placeholder: We are not building the merchant export API, even if the two enterprise renewals ask for it.

rubric.text: A specific, nameable thing someone could hold you to in November, and it names who wants it.
A specific thing, no stakeholder named.
Nothing actually ruled out ("we'll revisit as capacity allows"), or blank.

examples.text: We are not building SSO for the mid-market tier this year, even though two account managers have it in their renewal plans.
We are not building SSO for the mid-market tier this year.
We are deprioritizing the lower-impact enterprise requests.
We will revisit other requests as capacity allows.

reactive.headline: You are running someone else's roadmap.
reactive.body: Most of what you brought to the last planning cycle was shaped by whoever asked loudest. That is not a talent problem. Nobody told you the framing was the job. The first move is small: one direction for [initiative] that says what you are not doing.
reactive.next: Take a seat in the next cohort. You will bring one real decision from [initiative] each week and leave with a direction that says what you are not doing. If that feels like too much right now, start with the free exercise in your first email and the community.

emerging.headline: You set direction. It does not always hold.
emerging.body: You bring a point of view to [initiative], and then the same decision comes back a month later, because a trade-off stayed unnamed or a stakeholder family was never in the room. This is the band the cohort is built for: one real decision a week, tested until it holds.
emerging.next: This is the band the cohort is built for. Bring the decision on [initiative] that keeps coming back and we test it until it holds.

strategic.headline: Your framing travels. Now make it compound.
strategic.body: People repeat your direction for [initiative] back to you close to intact, and your trade-offs mostly stay decided. What is left is consistency across rooms and the one dimension that scored lowest. That is usually where a senior PM's next level lives.
strategic.next: The cohort gives you six weeks of pressure on your lowest dimension, from peers who will not let a trade-off stay vague. If 1:1 work is what you are after, book the review and we decide together.

leader.headline: You create gravity. The question is your team.
leader.body: Your answers on [initiative] describe someone whose direction holds without them in the room. At this level the leverage is in the PMs around you, and whether they can do what you just did.
leader.next: Take a seat, or send a PM on your team who should take this score. I run the same method with product teams; the review call is where we scope that.

dimensionCopy.orient: Orient is setting the direction before anyone hands you one. Your answers say the direction for [initiative] is a theme more than a choice. A choice rules something out. Try writing it again with the sentence "which means we are not" in the middle.
dimensionCopy.reframe: Reframe is changing how the room sees the problem without winning an argument. Your answers say you tend to answer the question as asked. Next time a stakeholder pushes, write down their frame in their words before you respond, and name who loses if the frame changes.
dimensionCopy.balance: Balance is saying what you are choosing against, before someone makes you. Your answers say your trade-offs on [initiative] have one real option in them. Write option B so a sane peer would pick it, then say plainly what you are not doing and who wanted it.
dimensionCopy.integrate: Integrate is carrying every function in one plan instead of winning each conversation separately. Your answers say one stakeholder family (usually finance or legal) meets [initiative] late. Ask each of them this week what would stop the launch.
dimensionCopy.transmit: Transmit is making the framing simple enough to travel without you. Your answers say the strategy for [initiative] lives in your head or in the features. Write the two-minute version, then have someone repeat it back and rewrite from what they got wrong.

intro.eyebrow: For senior PMs who own a roadmap
intro.h1: How does your judgment hold up when it's your roadmap on the line?
intro.p: Twelve questions about the initiative you actually own, scored against the five behaviors I see in PMs with real pull in their orgs: Orient, Reframe, Balance, Integrate, Transmit. You get a score out of 30, your weakest dimension, and a two-minute note from me for where you landed.
intro.muted: About four minutes. Every option is something a good PM would do, so answer with what happened, not what you'd like to have done.

copy.setupLabel: The initiative, in a few words
copy.setupError: A few words is enough, but I need something to write the questions around.

gate.h2: Where should I send the breakdown?
gate.p: Your score, your weakest dimension, and a short note from me arrive in a minute. Then a few emails over the next two weeks, one per dimension. Unsubscribe any time.

scoring.p: Reading your two sentences against the rubric. Ten seconds or so.

results.videoH3: Two minutes from me on the {band} band
results.videoP: What this band looks like in a planning meeting, the move to try this week, and what I'd do next.

meta.description: Twelve questions about the initiative you own, scored against the five ORBIT behaviors. Four minutes. From Josh Atlas, Product Management Circle.
